mainEntity.name: Should I shoot in monochrome mode in-camera?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes for the live view, no for the recorded file. Set your picture profile to monochrome so the live view, electronic viewfinder, and JPEG preview show the scene in black and white — this trains pre-visualisation. But shoot RAW so the file retains full colour information. RAW + mono picture profile gives you the best of both worlds: you see in monochrome at capture, but you have full colour data for the channel-slider work in post that's where most B&W craft happens. JPEG-only monochrome locks you out of that flexibility and is rarely the right choice unless you're shooting JPEG-only for a specific reason.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between desaturation and a proper B&W conversion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Desaturation just sets all colour channels to zero saturation — the result is technically monochrome but tonally flat and uniform. Proper B&W conversion uses the colour information to make tonal decisions: darken blues to deepen skies, lighten oranges to flatter skin, darken greens to add weight to foliage, lighten yellows to brighten highlights. Lightroom, Capture One and Silver Efex all let you adjust each colour channel's brightness independently in the B&W conversion. The same colour photograph can produce wildly different B&W conversions depending on how those channels are weighted — and that's where craft lives. Default desaturation is the worst possible B&W conversion.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if a scene will work in B&W before clicking?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three field tests. First, the camera mono preview — switch the picture profile to monochrome and look at the scene through the live view or EVF. If the live view image is more graphic and powerful than the colour version, the frame will likely convert well. Second, the squint test — half-close your eyes and look at the actual scene; squinting reduces colour information and approximates monochrome. Third, the contrast test — identify the brightest and darkest areas; if there's strong tonal separation between them, the scene has the contrast skeleton B&W needs. Scenes that fail all three tests aren't B&W candidates regardless of how the conversion is processed in post.

mainEntity.name: What kind of light is best for black-and-white photography?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anything with directional contrast and tonal variation. Hard side-light, backlight with subject silhouettes, low-angle morning or evening light raking across textured surfaces, broken cloud light with shafts hitting selected parts of the landscape — all of these produce the tonal separation B&W needs. Flat overcast light without strong shadows is generally the weakest B&W condition because there's no tonal skeleton to build from — though it can work for very simple high-key compositions or atmospheric subjects like mist and fog. Hard midday sun, often considered the worst light for colour landscape work, can be excellent for B&W because the harsh shadow contrast becomes a feature rather than a problem.

mainEntity.name: Should I add grain to my black-and-white conversions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sparingly, and with intent. Grain references the look of analogue film stocks (Tri-X, HP5, Delta 400) and can lend a B&W image a journalistic, documentary or fine-art-print character that pure digital cleanliness lacks. But applied without thought, grain becomes a generic Instagram-filter affectation that adds nothing. Two practical rules: keep the amount low (5–15 in Lightroom's grain slider is usually plenty), and match the grain to the subject — heavier grain suits street, reportage and gritty subjects; lighter or no grain suits fine-art landscape and architectural work. Never use grain to disguise a soft or noisy frame; it doesn't fix the underlying problem and tends to amplify it.

mainEntity.name: Why does my black-and-white work look flat and grey?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always one of three causes. First, the original scene didn't have enough tonal contrast to support B&W — a flat-light woodland or overcast meadow has no skeleton to build from regardless of how it's processed. Second, the conversion is using default desaturation rather than channel-aware conversion — adjusting individual colour-channel brightness adds the tonal separation that desaturation removes. Third, the black point and white point aren't set — a strong B&W image typically has a deep true-black somewhere and a clean true-white somewhere, even if those are small areas. If your B&W histograms cluster in the middle without reaching either end, the image will read as muddy grey rather than tonally rich.

mainEntity.name: Is film black-and-white different from digital black-and-white?

acceptedAnswer.text: In look, yes — there's a tonal character to silver-halide film B&W (the way Tri-X handles highlight roll-off, the way Ilford HP5 renders mid-tones, the grain structure of Kodak T-Max) that digital approximates rather than reproduces. In decision-making and creative principles, no — the question of whether a scene works in monochrome and why it works is the same regardless of medium. Modern digital B&W tools (Silver Efex Pro, Lightroom's film simulation profiles, Capture One's styles) can closely emulate specific film stocks, and many photographers shoot digital RAW and process to match a specific film look. Whether to shoot actual film or emulate it digitally is a creative and workflow decision; the underlying B&W decisions in this article apply equally to either path.

mainEntity.name: How do I know when to stop processing a B&W image?

acceptedAnswer.text: When the image looks like a photograph rather than a B&W treatment. The harsh, crunchy, over-clarified, blown-highlight-and-crushed-shadow aesthetic that's become a digital B&W cliché is the modern equivalent of HDR overcooking — it dates an image faster than any colour grading would. Practical rules: keep contrast and clarity moderate (Lightroom contrast +10 to +25, clarity +5 to +20 is usually plenty); preserve detail in both highlights and shadows even when pushing tonal range; let the original scene's tonal structure carry the photograph rather than processing trying to manufacture drama that wasn't there at capture. The strongest B&W conversions usually look like the photograph could plausibly have been printed in a darkroom — restrained, tonal, considered.
